title: Linux Fundamentals
summary: Linux is the operating system that runs virtually all production infrastructure. Understanding its filesystem layout, permissions model, process management, and package system is the foundation everything else in DevOps builds on.

sections.title: The Linux filesystem hierarchy
sections.body:
## What is the Linux filesystem hierarchy?

On Windows, each storage device gets its own drive letter (`C:`, `D:`). Linux takes a fundamentally different approach: **everything hangs off a single tree rooted at `/`**, called the root directory. Physical disks, network shares, USB drives, and even virtual kernel interfaces all appear as directories somewhere inside that tree. This is called the **Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)**, and it was established so that any Linux admin who sits down at an unfamiliar machine immediately knows where to find things.

Understanding this layout is not just academic — it determines where you look when something breaks. Applications write their config to `/etc/`, log their errors to `/var/log/`, store their binaries in `/usr/bin/` or `/usr/local/bin/`, and expose live runtime state through `/proc/` and `/sys/`. If you don't know the tree, you'll waste time hunting.

**Key directories every DevOps engineer must know:**

- **`/etc/`** — All system-wide configuration lives here as plain text files. This is the most important directory for operations. Misconfigured files here are the cause of the majority of "the service won't start" incidents.
- **`/var/`** — Variable data: logs (`/var/log/`), mail spools, package caches. Grows over time and can fill disks if not monitored.
- **`/proc/` and `/sys/`** — These are *virtual* filesystems. Nothing is stored on disk; the kernel generates the content on the fly. Reading `/proc/cpuinfo` queries the CPU, not a file.
- **`/usr/`** — Read-only user programs and libraries. `/usr/bin/` for distribution packages, `/usr/local/bin/` for things you install manually.
- **`/opt/`** — Self-contained third-party software bundles. A program installed here typically brings all its own dependencies.
- **`/tmp/`** — Ephemeral scratch space, cleared on every reboot. Never store anything here you care about.
- **`/dev/`** — Device files. `/dev/null` discards everything written to it. `/dev/sda` is the first SATA disk. `/dev/random` generates cryptographic random bytes.

**Why it matters for DevOps:** Container images, Kubernetes pods, and CI runners all run Linux. When a container fails, you need to know where to look — is the problem a missing config in `/etc/`? A full disk in `/var/`? A missing binary in `/usr/bin/`? The FHS is your map.

Linux follows the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS). Every file lives under `/` (root). Knowing what lives where stops you from getting lost.

```
/
├── bin/     → essential user binaries (ls, cp, bash)
├── sbin/    → system binaries (reboot, fdisk)
├── etc/     → configuration files — the most important directory for ops
├── var/     → variable data: logs (/var/log), spool, cache
├── home/    → user home directories (/home/esteban)
├── root/    → root user's home
├── tmp/     → temporary files, cleared on reboot
├── usr/     → read-only user data; usr/bin, usr/local/bin for installed programs
├── opt/     → optional software packages (self-contained installations)
├── proc/    → virtual filesystem: running kernel and process info
├── sys/     → virtual filesystem: device and kernel info
├── dev/     → device files (disks, terminals, /dev/null, /dev/random)
├── lib/     → shared libraries for /bin and /sbin
└── mnt/     → temporary mount points
```

The ones you'll touch most in DevOps:

```bash
# Configuration — edit with care
ls /etc/apt/             # apt config (nginx not installed in sandbox)
ls /etc/systemd/system/  # systemd service files
cat /etc/hosts           # local hostname resolution
cat /etc/resolv.conf     # DNS resolver config

# Logs — your first stop when something breaks
tail /var/log/dpkg.log 2>/dev/null | head -5  # package install log
# journalctl requires systemd — not available in containers (use kubectl logs instead)

# Kernel and hardware info via /proc
cat /proc/cpuinfo     # CPU details
cat /proc/meminfo     # memory details
cat /proc/version     # kernel version
```

sections.title: Users, groups, and permissions
sections.body:
## Understanding Linux permissions

Linux was designed from the beginning as a **multi-user operating system**. The permissions system is the mechanism the kernel uses to enforce boundaries between users and protect the system from accidental or malicious damage. Every file and directory has an owner (a user), a group, and a set of permission bits. The kernel checks these on every file operation.

**The three permission classes:**

- **Owner (user)** — the person or process that created the file
- **Group** — a named collection of users; files can be group-shared
- **Other** — everyone else on the system

**The three permission bits per class:**

| Bit | Symbolic | Numeric | Meaning on a file | Meaning on a directory |
|-----|----------|---------|-------------------|------------------------|
| read | `r` | 4 | View file contents | List directory contents (`ls`) |
| write | `w` | 2 | Modify file | Create/delete/rename files inside |
| execute | `x` | 1 | Run as a program | Enter the directory (`cd`) |

**How numeric modes work:** Each class's three bits add up to a single digit (0–7). `rwx` = 4+2+1 = **7**. `r-x` = 4+0+1 = **5**. `rw-` = 4+2+0 = **6**. So `755` means owner=rwx, group=r-x, other=r-x — the standard for executable scripts and directories. `644` means owner=rw-, group=r--, other=r-- — the standard for config files and static assets.

**Why this matters in DevOps:** Misconfigured permissions cause two types of problems. Too restrictive: the application can't read its config, write its logs, or listen on a port — and silently fails. Too permissive: a world-writable config file, or a setuid binary, becomes a security hole. Every time you deploy a new service, setting the right owner and mode on its files is a required step, not an afterthought.

**Principle of least privilege:** A web server running as `www-data` should own its static files but should not be able to read `/etc/shadow`. A database process should own its data directory but shouldn't be able to write to `/usr/bin/`. Applying this principle limits the blast radius if a process is compromised.

Linux permissions determine who can read, write, or execute a file. Getting these wrong is a common cause of both broken deployments and security incidents.

```bash
# ls -l output format:
# -rwxr-xr-- 1 alice devs 4096 Jan 1 10:00 script.sh
#  ^^^^^^^^^
#  |└──┬──┘└──┬──┘└──┬──┘
#  |   │      │      └── other: r-- (read only)
#  |   │      └──────── group: r-x (read + execute)
#  |   └─────────────── owner: rwx (read + write + execute)
#  └─────────────────── file type (- file, d dir, l symlink)

# Each permission set: r=4, w=2, x=1
# rwxr-xr-- = 7 5 4 = 754

# chmod — change permissions
chmod 755 /workspace/check_images.py   # rwxr-xr-x  (owner: all, group: r+x, other: r+x)
chmod 644 /workspace/config.yaml       # rw-r--r--  (owner: r+w, group: r, other: r)
chmod -R 755 /workspace               # recursive

# chown — change owner
chown root /workspace/config.yaml  # running as root already

# Users and groups
id                    # show current user, uid, gid, groups
whoami                # just the username
groups                # show groups you belong to

# sudo — run as root
apt update -qq 2>/dev/null | tail -1

# Special permissions
# setuid (4xxx): run as file owner, not caller — used by /usr/bin/passwd
# setgid (2xxx): run as file group
# sticky bit (1xxx): only owner can delete — used on /tmp
ls -la /tmp | head -3  # drwxrwxrwt ← t = sticky bit
```

Key principle: **least privilege**. Application processes should run as a dedicated non-root user with only the permissions they need.

sections.title: Process management
sections.body:
## What is a process?

When you run a command, the operating system creates a **process** — an isolated, running instance of a program. Each process gets its own block of memory, a unique **PID (Process ID)**, a set of open file descriptors, and a record of the user it's running as. The kernel is the traffic controller: it schedules CPU time, enforces memory boundaries, and handles signals between processes.

**Process relationships:** Every process (except PID 1, the init system) has a **parent process (PPID)**. When a shell runs a command, the shell forks a child process to execute it. When a program calls `fork()`, it creates a copy of itself. This tree structure is how Linux organizes all running software.

**Process states:** At any moment a process is in one of several states:
- **R** (Running or Runnable) — currently using or waiting for CPU
- **S** (Sleeping) — waiting for I/O, a timer, or a signal; most processes spend their time here
- **D** (Uninterruptible Sleep) — waiting for disk I/O; a high count of D-state processes signals an I/O problem
- **Z** (Zombie) — process finished but parent hasn't collected its exit code yet
- **T** (Stopped) — paused by a signal (e.g., `Ctrl+Z`)

**Signals:** The primary way to communicate with processes. A signal is a small integer sent to a process by the kernel or another process. The most important ones:
- **SIGTERM (15)** — politely ask the process to shut down; the process can catch this and clean up
- **SIGKILL (9)** — force-kill immediately; the process cannot catch or ignore this
- **SIGHUP (1)** — originally "terminal hangup," now commonly used to tell daemons to reload their config
- **SIGINT (2)** — what `Ctrl+C` sends

**Load average explained:** The three numbers shown by `uptime` and `top` (e.g., `0.52 0.41 0.38`) represent the average number of runnable + D-state processes over the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes. On a 4-core machine, a load average of 4.0 means all cores are fully busy. Above that and work is queuing up.

**Why process management matters in DevOps:** Services crash, leak memory, and deadlock. You need to be able to find a runaway process, check its resource usage, send it the right signal to reload or restart, and understand why it entered a bad state — all without disrupting other processes on the same host.

Every running program is a process with a PID (process ID). DevOps work constantly involves starting, stopping, and inspecting processes.

```bash
# View processes
ps aux                   # all processes, BSD style
ps aux | grep nginx      # find nginx processes
ps -ef --forest          # tree view showing parent/child

# top / htop — interactive process viewer
top                  # CPU, memory, load average, per-process view
# In top: press M (sort by memory), P (sort by CPU), k (kill), q (quit)
# htop is the friendlier version — try: htop

# Key process info
# PID   # process ID — used to signal/kill
# PPID  # parent PID
# UID   # user running the process
# CPU%  # CPU usage
# MEM%  # memory usage
# STAT  # state: R(running), S(sleeping), Z(zombie), D(disk wait)

# Signals
kill -0 $$ 2>/dev/null && echo "process $$ exists"  # -0 checks existence without killing
kill -1 1234    # SIGHUP: reload config (used by nginx, sshd)
pkill -0 nginx 2>/dev/null && echo nginx running || echo nginx not running
pkill -f pattern # kill processes matching a pattern

# Background and foreground
sleep 5 &           # run in background
jobs                # list background jobs
# fg/bg require interactive shell (job control); fg 1 / bg 1
nohup sleep 3 &    # keep running after logout

# systemd — the modern way to manage services
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl status nginx        # show status
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl start nginx         # start service
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl stop nginx          # stop service
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl restart nginx       # restart (stop + start)
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl reload nginx        # reload config without restart
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl enable nginx        # start automatically at boot
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl disable nginx       # remove autostart
# systemctl not available in containers: systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running  # list running services
```

sections.title: Package management & software installation
sections.body:
## How package management works

Software on Linux is distributed as **packages** — archives containing binaries, libraries, config files, and metadata (name, version, dependencies, maintainer). A **package manager** handles downloading, verifying, installing, upgrading, and removing packages while automatically resolving their dependency trees.

**Why package managers exist:** Manually installing software means tracking where files were placed, what version is installed, and whether all dependencies are satisfied. When you have hundreds of servers, doing this by hand is impossible. Package managers create a reproducible, auditable record of exactly what software is installed on each machine.

**The package manager landscape:**

| Distro family | Package manager | Package format | Config location |
|---------------|-----------------|----------------|-----------------|
| Debian / Ubuntu | `apt` (high-level), `dpkg` (low-level) | `.deb` | `/etc/apt/` |
| RHEL / CentOS / Rocky | `dnf` or `yum` | `.rpm` | `/etc/yum.repos.d/` |
| Alpine Linux | `apk` | `.apk` | `/etc/apk/` |
| Arch Linux | `pacman` | `.pkg.tar.zst` | `/etc/pacman.conf` |

**How `apt` works internally:** When you run `apt update`, apt downloads index files from the configured repositories (listed in `/etc/apt/sources.list`) and stores them locally. When you run `apt install nginx`, apt looks up nginx in those indexes, resolves all its dependencies, downloads the `.deb` files, verifies their GPG signatures, and calls `dpkg` to unpack and install them.

**Package repositories vs. manual installation:** Not every tool you need in DevOps lives in the official package repos. Tools like `kubectl`, `helm`, `terraform`, `argocd`, and `flux` are often distributed as static binaries or tarballs from their project's GitHub releases. The common pattern is: download the binary, verify its checksum (SHA256), mark it executable with `chmod +x`, and move it to `/usr/local/bin/` so it's on your `PATH`.

**In containers:** Docker images are built layer by layer, and each `RUN apt install` command adds a layer. DevOps best practice is to install only what the application needs (minimizing attack surface and image size) and to pin package versions so builds are reproducible.

Different Linux distributions use different package managers. Debian/Ubuntu use `apt`, RHEL/CentOS use `yum`/`dnf`, Alpine uses `apk`.

```bash norun
# ── Debian / Ubuntu (apt) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Update package list (always do this first)
apt update

# Install a package
apt install -y nginx curl git

# Remove a package
apt remove nginx
apt purge nginx      # also removes config files

# Search for a package
apt search nginx

# Show package info
apt show nginx

# Upgrade all installed packages
apt upgrade -y

# ── RHEL / CentOS / Rocky (yum / dnf) ─────────────────────────────────────
yum install -y nginx
dnf install -y nginx   # newer RHEL/CentOS 8+

# ── Alpine (used in Docker images) ────────────────────────────────────────
apk add nginx curl git
apk del nginx

# ── Installing from binary / tarball ──────────────────────────────────────
# Many DevOps tools aren't in package managers
# Pattern: download, verify, install to /usr/local/bin
curl -LO https://dl.k8s.io/release/v1.29.4/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl
chmod +x kubectl
mv kubectl /usr/local/bin/

# Pattern: extract tarball
tar -xzf tool-v1.0.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz
mv tool /usr/local/bin/

# Check what's installed
which kubectl       # find the binary
kubectl version     # confirm it works
dpkg -l | grep nginx  # list installed debian packages
rpm -qa | grep nginx  # list installed rpm packages
```

In Docker containers, the image typically uses `apt` or `apk`. In the sandbox backend container (Debian-based), `apt` is available but most tools are pre-installed.

sections.title: Exercise: explore the sandbox Linux environment
sections.body:
## Putting it all together: exploring a live Linux system

The best way to internalize the Linux filesystem, permissions, and process model is to observe them in a running system. This exercise has you answer concrete questions about the sandbox environment by reading from the kernel's own interfaces — `/proc`, `/etc`, and the process table.

As you work through these commands, pay attention to the *shape* of the output. The format of `id`, `ps aux`, `df -h`, and `cat /proc/version` is consistent across every Linux system you'll ever work on. Muscle memory for reading this output will serve you in every production incident.

**Key things to notice:**
- The Linux distribution and kernel version tell you what packages and kernel features are available
- The user you're running as determines what files you can read and what commands you can run
- Memory and disk statistics show you the resource envelope you're operating within
- The process table tells you what software is actually running, not just what's configured to run
- `/proc/<pid>/` gives you a window into any running process's internals

Use the terminal to answer the following questions about the sandbox environment:

```bash
# 1. What Linux distribution and kernel version is running?
cat /etc/os-release
uname -r

# 2. What user are you running as? What groups?
id

# 3. How much memory is available? How much disk?
free -h
df -h /

# 4. What processes are using the most CPU right now?
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -10

# 5. Find all files in /workspace
find /workspace -type f
ls -la /workspace

# 6. Inspect the /etc directory — what config files exist?
ls /etc | head -20

# 7. Check which tools are installed and where they live
which kubectl helm argocd python3 jq

# 8. Look at the running services (systemd is not used here — Docker)
# Instead, see what processes are running:
ps aux | grep -v grep

# 9. Find the kubeconfig file and examine it (without printing sensitive data)
ls -la /tmp/k3s.yaml
cat /tmp/k3s.yaml | grep -v 'certificate\|key'

# 10. Check disk usage of the /data directory
du -sh /data/*
```

**Bonus:** The `/proc` filesystem is live kernel data. Try:

```bash
cat /proc/1/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '    # what is PID 1 running?
ls /proc/ | grep '^[0-9]' | wc -l   # how many processes exist?
cat /proc/meminfo | grep MemTotal    # total memory in kB
```
